overall: From the domain-transfer perspective the proposal makes the main cut correctly: it transfers no board, no authority chain, no worksheet, and no new record type, and its fact base is mostly accurate (of 25 checks, 9 CORRECT, 10 PARTLY, 6 UNVERIFIED, none wholly wrong; quotations from NASA directives, the Rogers report, the SRE books, Nygard, and the RFCs are exact). It still fails in four places where an aerospace assumption survives the reduction. First, clause 7.4 (c) assumes that a lapsed waiver stops the activity; in software the departure continues, and the rule plus example 5 hide it. Second, 7.3 (h) keeps the record of dissent while dropping the escalation right and non-retribution duty that make Formal Dissent work, and the cited case was a written objection that did not travel, not an unwritten one. Third, the levels classify per record by the author, whereas every cited precedent classifies by category in advance, and 'cannot be undone' without magnitude makes trivial irreversible actions critical. Fourth, the claim-versus-choice split and the named risk acceptor presuppose separate certifying and deciding bodies and collapse to boilerplate in a small team. The proposal also underuses native software forms it cites: the pre-stated canary abort criterion, error budgets, change categories, and inline suppressions with expiry. Its three 'findings that shaped the design' are each stated more firmly than the sources support: the lowest NASA classes were not inspected, the shuttle reports describe propagation and authority failures at least as much as record failures, and SRE chapter 32 concerns per-service onboarding and ends in frameworks, not in abandoning review. On the evidence, adopt the 4.6 sentence, 7.3 (i), the templates, and the guide text; treat the rest of section 7 as anticipated-only or deferred until an adopter has used it.

clause_verdicts.reason: This is the one item whose native software form (the ADR context section, verified in Nygard today) is older and better tested than any aerospace form, and it does not depend on authority chains, boards, or irreversibility. The escape clause keeps clause 3.3.3 intact. It is breaking and it binds trivial tracked decisions, but the cost is one line. It should be released on its own merits and not bundled with section 7.

The clause says what the profile does not require but not that existing engineering artifacts can be the record. In software the evidence, rollout plan, abort criteria, and examination already live in the pull request, pipeline run, rollout configuration, alert rule, and ticket. Without saying so, 7.3 will be read as a document to write, which duplicates native artifacts and breaks the brief's no-duplication constraint.
clause_verdicts.replacement: 7.1 Use this profile when a project wants a later reader to be able to reconstruct, for its consequential decisions, changes, exceptions, and incidents: what was believed, on what evidence, which risks were accepted and by whom, and what happened afterwards. The profile states what a record makes discoverable. A pull request, change ticket, pipeline run, or other native artifact is a sufficient record where it makes the content discoverable (clause 3.6.1); no separate document is required. The profile does not require that a review be held, that a role be staffed, or that a change be approved (clause 3.6.3), and it requires nothing at the routine level. It can be used with or without tracked records.

clause_verdicts.reason: Every cited precedent classifies in advance by category (NASA: the system or subsystem, once; SRE chapter 27: 'no new server executables and a traffic increase under 10%'; ITIL: a standard-change catalogue). The proposal instead has an author classify each decision. In continuous delivery that is a judgment made dozens of times a day by the person with most incentive to say 'routine'. The transferable abstraction is criteria stated as kinds of change, so that routine work is never individually classified.
clause_verdicts.replacement: 7.2 (a) A project applying this profile MUST state in its adoption note which kinds of decision or change it treats as significant and which as critical, and who may assign a level to a case the list does not cover. Everything else is routine.

clause_verdicts.reason: Stating level and deciding factor on a record that already exists is cheap and detectable. It is only reached for non-routine records.

'Higher wins' is rational for NASA because classification happens once per system and the cost is borne once. Applied per change with the proposed definition of critical (any effect that 'cannot be undone'), it ratchets ordinary irreversible actions to critical: sending an email, publishing a package version, deleting a temporary table, rotating a key. Irreversibility without magnitude is not criticality in software. The tie rule should not be a SHOULD (clause 1.2 then demands a reason for every departure); the definition of critical needs a magnitude term.
clause_verdicts.replacement: 7.2 (c) Critical is reserved for a change whose wrong outcome would be material outside the deciding team and could not be undone, detected, or contained by present means. Irreversibility of an effect that is immaterial does not raise the level. A project MAY map existing local classes, such as change types or severity classes, to these levels.

clause_verdicts.reason: (a) 'the claim ... stated separately from the choice' transfers a structure that is rational where a board certifies readiness and a different authority decides (FRR). In a team where the author, the claimant, and the decider are one person in one pull request, the claim degenerates to 'the change is ready', as the proposal's own example 2 shows ('claim: migration is ready'). That line carries no information; the information is in (b). (d) 'who accepted them' presumes a risk owner distinct from the decider; in a small team it is always the 4.6 authority, so it becomes a repeated name. (e) is the strongest and most native item. Missing from the list is the native software equivalent of success criteria: the observation that will cause the rollout to be stopped or undone, decided beforehand. That is what a canary evaluation is, and it is more useful than a readiness claim.
clause_verdicts.replacement: 7.3 A record of a decision to make or proceed with a change at the significant or critical level MUST make the following discoverable, on the page or through links: (a) the evidence that the change will work, and what that evidence does not cover; (b) the assumptions relied on; (c) the known risks that remain, and who accepted them where that is not the authority named under clause 4.6; (d) how the effect will be undone or contained, or that it cannot be; (e) what observation would cause the change to be stopped or undone.

clause_verdicts.reason: 'How the change could fail and how the failure would be detected' is the FMEA question reduced to prose; the reduction is right, but placing it at critical only inverts software economics. Detection is the cheap, native part (alert rules, canary metrics, error budgets) and is most useful exactly for the significant changes that are reversible only if someone notices. Fold the detection half into the significant list as the stop criterion (see replacement for 7.3 (a)-(e), item e) and keep the open-ended 'how could it fail' prompt as guide advice for critical changes, where it cannot be checked for adequacy anyway.

Disclosure of who examined, or that no one did, transfers cleanly: it needs no Technical Authority, works for a solo maintainer ('no one'), and maps to the native form (review on the pull request, linked). It is the honest residue of IV&V. Add to the guide that a link to the review thread satisfies it.

The home-domain mechanism (NPR 7120.5F 3.4, read today) has three working parts: a duty of non-retribution, a documented dissent, and a right to carry it at least two levels up, to the Administrator if needed. The proposal transfers only the middle one. In the cited case the dissent was already written (Rogers p. 82 names an 'initial written recommendation'); what failed was that it did not reach the deciders. A record rule does not address that. Without protection or an upward path, a MUST that binds only 'disagreement recorded before acceptance' rewards keeping disagreement oral, and its violation cannot be seen from the page (the proposal admits detection needs comparison with drafts). The admission test then says it is not a MUST.
clause_verdicts.replacement: Move to the decision guide, which already says 'Record dissent or an unresolved assumption if it could change the choice', and add: 'Where a disagreement that could change the choice was raised before acceptance, the record SHOULD state it and why it did not prevail.' Keep the sentence 'The absence of recorded disagreement does not establish agreement.' in 7.3.

clause_verdicts.reason: The smallest and most transferable abstraction in the package. It needs no organization, applies to any team size, and is the software-native lesson too (a quiet canary proves nothing if the metric could not have shown the fault). It should survive even if the rest of section 7 is deferred; it could be one sentence in the decision guide pointing to clause 5.7.

'An exception MUST identify ...' with 'exception' defined as any accepted departure from 'a requirement the project otherwise treats as binding' captures every native software exception mechanism: lint and type-check suppressions, skipped tests, vulnerability-scanner ignore entries, policy-as-code allowlists, branch-protection bypasses. A waiver form per item is rational when there are tens of waivers per vehicle and each is a hardware nonconformance; it is absurd for four hundred suppressions. Software already has a better native form: the suppression at the point of departure, carrying a reason and, in many tools, an expiry. The clause must bound itself to requirements stated in the corpus and let the native artifact be the record.
clause_verdicts.replacement: 7.4 (a) An exception to a requirement stated in the corpus MUST make discoverable the requirement departed from, its scope, the reason, the risk accepted, who accepted it, and an expiry date or review condition. An entry in a native mechanism, such as a suppression or allowlist file, is a sufficient record where it carries or links these.

clause_verdicts.reason: Sound advice (the NPR 7120.5F Non-Applicable ruling is the precedent, verified today) but a SHOULD costs a recorded reason on each departure (clause 1.2) and nothing detectable is gained. It is a template prompt and already appears in the proposed exception outline.
clause_verdicts.replacement: Guidance only: keep the prompt in templates/exception.md.

clause_verdicts.reason: This is the clearest transfer failure in the package. At NASA a waiver that is not renewed means the vehicle does not fly; the departure stops with the waiver. In software the system keeps running after the date: the legacy service still does not rotate credentials. Example 5 says that after expiry 'the index of exceptions in force no longer lists it'. The departure is then still happening and has become invisible, which is exactly the Rogers finding 2 failure (a waiver not visible to all levels) produced by the rule meant to prevent it. The rule must keep an expired exception more visible, not less.
clause_verdicts.replacement: 7.4 (c) An exception whose expiry date has passed without a recorded renewal MUST be shown as lapsed: it MUST NOT be presented as accepted, and it MUST NOT be removed from where exceptions are listed while the departure continues.

clause_verdicts.reason: Visibility at the requirement is the part Rogers finding 2 actually supports. For software the fixed label plus search is the native equivalent and is enough. Keep as SHOULD.

Disposition per lesson is the native software form (postmortem action items) and transfers without any corrective-action board. Two defects. 'A change pending, with a link to where it is tracked' has no end and is the standard way action items die; a date costs nothing. And forcing a disposition on every 'lesson' gives authors a reason to list fewer lessons or to phrase observations as non-lessons; the rule should bind proposed actions, not insights.
clause_verdicts.replacement: 7.5 (a) A record of an incident investigation MUST state, for each change it recommends, one disposition: made, with a link to it; pending, with a link to where it is tracked and the date it will next be looked at; not made, with the reason and who accepted the remaining risk.

clause_verdicts.reason: Linking the incident to the decision whose assumption failed is cheap and is the one place the profile closes the loop. SHOULD is right; it only applies where a recorded decision exists.

'When and how its outcome will be checked' is the aerospace post-flight assessment review transplanted. In software the outcome check of a rollout is the rollout itself (canary evaluation, error budget burn, alerts), already covered by the stop criterion; for irreversible one-off actions it duplicates 7.3 (d). The proposal names it as first to drop and reports no observed case.

candidates.strongest_objection: The principle is sound in every domain, but in its home domains proportionality is achieved by classifying a system or a category of change once, in advance, by someone other than the author (NPR 7150.2D Appendix D; SRE chapter 27 low-risk category). The proposal turns it into a per-decision judgment by the author. The cited SRE chapter 32 evidence is about per-service onboarding reviews, not per-change review, so it does not show what the proposal says it shows.
candidates.counterexample: A team of four deploys thirty times a day. If each deploy needs a moment's thought about level, the tax is thirty classifications a day for nothing; if it does not, the level is decided by habit and the one dangerous change in the batch (a schema change hidden in a dependency bump) is routine by default.
candidates.gaming: Everything is declared routine; the profile is 'adopted' and requires nothing.
candidates.recommended_change: State the principle in foundations.md as proposed, and make 7.2 (a) classify by kind of change (see clause verdict).

candidates.strongest_objection: No domain-transfer objection: this is native software practice (ADR). The only overreach is citing Nygard for 'rationale'; his format has Context and Consequences and no rationale field.
candidates.counterexample: A decision made by an external authority (a regulator, a customer contract, a parent company) where the team genuinely does not know the reasons: handled by the escape 'not recorded'. None found beyond that.
candidates.gaming: 'Reasons: as discussed.' or a blanket 'not recorded' on every decision.
candidates.recommended_change: Adopt the 4.6 sentence on its own. In the guide, say that the reasons may be a link to the context section of an existing ADR.

candidates.strongest_objection: 'GO' is a readiness-board construct: a body certifies against stated criteria and a separate authority decides. That split is what makes a separately stated claim informative. Continuous delivery has a better native form: the gate is a pre-stated, usually automated, criterion (tests pass, canary within thresholds, error budget not exhausted) and GO is the pipeline's output. A prose 'claim' line beside it is redundant. NPR 7123.1D Appendix G, which the proposal cites, calls its criteria 'recommended best practices' and expects tailoring; it does not say what the proposal infers from it.
candidates.counterexample: Schema migration behind an automated pipeline: the evidence is the dry-run link and the gate is the pipeline. Writing 'Claim: the migration is ready' (the proposal's own example 2) adds a line that no reader will ever use, and trains authors to fill fields.
candidates.gaming: Claim: 'ready'. Evidence: 'CI green' with a link, whatever CI covers.
candidates.recommended_change: Drop 7.3 (a) as a separate item; keep evidence and its limits; add the stop or abort criterion as the native form of success criteria.

candidates.strongest_objection: Waivers in aerospace are few, per vehicle or per requirement, dispositioned by a standing authority, and a lapsed waiver grounds the vehicle. Software exceptions are numerous, live in code and configuration, and outlive any date because the system keeps running. NPR 7120.5F 3.5.1 (read today) calls tailoring 'both an expected and accepted part of establishing proper requirements'; the adversarial framing of exceptions comes from the accident reports, not from the process the proposal cites. In a five-person company 'who accepted the risk' is the founder every time, and the field stops carrying information.
candidates.counterexample: A repository with several hundred lint suppressions and scanner ignore entries, each technically an accepted departure from a binding rule. Giving each six fields in a decision record is worse than the native inline suppression with a reason; exempting them needs a line the proposal does not draw.
candidates.gaming: One umbrella exception: 'legacy services are exempt from current standards, accepted by the CTO, review annually'.
candidates.recommended_change: Bound 7.4 (a) to requirements stated in the corpus and accept native suppression mechanisms as the record.

candidates.strongest_objection: None on transfer; this is the one aerospace lesson that needs no aerospace organization, and the chaos-engineering and canary literature states the software-native form. The proposal's wording 'not from the absence of incidents' is attributed to principlesofchaos.org, which does not say it.
candidates.counterexample: none found: the rule is conditional and only asks an author who offers silence as evidence to say what was being listened to.
candidates.gaming: 'Monitored in production for two weeks; alerts would have fired', where no alert covers the failure in question.
candidates.recommended_change: Keep 7.3 (i). If section 7 is deferred, put the same sentence in the decision guide with a pointer to clause 5.7.

candidates.strongest_objection: FMEA is rational where failure modes are enumerable per component and hardware cannot be patched. For a software change the enumerable part is small and the valuable, checkable part is detection: what signal, what threshold, what action. The proposal keeps the unenumerable half ('how the change could fail') as a MUST and restricts detection to critical changes, where it matters least relative to significant ones that are safe only if noticed.
candidates.counterexample: A feature-flag flip for one percent of users. 'How could it fail' has unbounded answers; the useful answer is 'error rate on the flagged cohort above X for five minutes turns the flag off', which is a detection and stop rule, not a failure analysis.
candidates.gaming: 'Could fail in unforeseen ways; standard monitoring applies.'
candidates.recommended_change: Replace 7.3 (f) with a stop criterion at significant level; keep 'how could it fail' as a guide prompt.

candidates.strongest_objection: The principle is native to software (rollback, flags, restore tests) and the proposal uses the native form. The weak spot is the GitLab citation: the postmortem's own answer to why backups were untested is 'there was no ownership', an organizational cause a record field does not fix, and the proposal misreports that the action list has owners.
candidates.counterexample: Roll-forward-only systems (event-sourced ledgers, published package versions, sent notifications): 'undo' is not the right question and a mechanical author writes 'cannot be undone', which under 7.2 (c) makes every such change critical.
candidates.gaming: 'Rollback: revert the commit', for a change with a data migration that the revert does not reverse.
candidates.recommended_change: Keep 7.3 (e). Word it 'undone, corrected forward, or contained' so that roll-forward systems are not forced to 'cannot be'.

candidates.strongest_objection: Technical Authority exists because a program manager under schedule pressure outranked the engineers; independence is funded separately (CAIB R7.5-2, read today: 'no connection to or responsibility for schedule or program cost'). A five-person company cannot construct that, and the proposal rightly does not try. But then the candidate as worded ('require independent challenge') is not delivered, and the proposal should say REJECTED-AS-WORDED, not NORMATIVE. What remains, disclosure, is fine.
candidates.counterexample: Solo maintainer of a widely used library making an irreversible release decision. 'Independent challenge' is impossible; the honest record is 'no one', and the rule works. Mechanical compliance failure is the opposite case: a team asks a colleague to 'take a look' at 16:55 so the field has a name in it.
candidates.gaming: A named examiner who approved the pull request in ninety seconds; or an automated agent's review listed without its limits.
candidates.recommended_change: Keep 7.3 (g) as disclosure. Record in the decision that P-08 as worded was not adopted and why.

candidates.strongest_objection: Formal Dissent at NASA works through an escalation right and a non-retribution duty; the record is a by-product. Transferring only the record to an organization with neither makes writing a dissent costly for the dissenter and easy to avoid for the decider. The observed case does not support a record rule: the Commission says the deciders were unaware of an 'initial written recommendation', so the dissent was on paper and still did not travel. RFC 7282 is Informational and about open working groups, not manager-led teams.
candidates.counterexample: An engineer objects in a design review. Knowing that written objections must appear in the accepted record with 'the reason it did not prevail', the lead asks to 'take it offline'; the objection is settled orally and never recorded. The rule has reduced the written trace.
candidates.gaming: 'Disagreement: none recorded.' Always true if nobody writes anything down.
candidates.recommended_change: Downgrade 7.3 (h) to a SHOULD in the guide; keep the 'absence does not establish agreement' sentence.

candidates.strongest_objection: Corrective-action tracking in aerospace is a system with closure authority. The software-native form, postmortem action items in the ordinary tracker, is better and the proposal uses it. The strong form of the candidate (not closed until the system changes) is a process rule the proposal rightly drops. Remaining objection: binding every 'lesson' to a disposition penalizes writing down insights that have no action, which blameless-review practice values (prior knowledge, not inspected). The SRE 'unreviewed postmortem' quotation is misapplied as support.
candidates.counterexample: A postmortem notes 'operators did not know the dashboard existed'. As a lesson it now needs a disposition and a link; the author deletes the sentence instead.
candidates.gaming: Every lesson 'pending', linked to a ticket that is later closed as stale.
candidates.recommended_change: Bind recommended changes, not lessons; add a next-look date to 'pending' (see 7.5 (a) replacement).

candidates.strongest_objection: Three levels is a reasonable minimum, but the definitions transfer the aerospace weight on irreversibility without the aerospace weight on magnitude. In software many irreversible effects are trivial and many reversible ones are catastrophic before they are reversed (a reversible configuration push that takes down authentication for an hour). And every cited precedent assigns the class by category in advance, not per record by its author.
candidates.counterexample: Sending a one-off email to fifty beta users cannot be undone, so it is critical by definition and by the 7.2 (c) tie rule: examiner, dissent, failure analysis. Meanwhile a global configuration change with a tested rollback is merely significant.
candidates.gaming: Split a critical change into several 'significant' ones, or classify at the level of the pull request instead of the release.
candidates.recommended_change: Define critical by magnitude and irreversibility together; state criteria as kinds of change; drop the 'higher SHOULD' rule in favour of the definition.

candidates.strongest_objection: The nine-field structure is an assurance-case skeleton. ISO/IEC/IEEE 15026-2 (not inspected by anyone here) describes a maintained argument about a system property, kept current over the system's life. A per-change field list is a different thing, and citing the standard for it lends authority the standard does not give. As fields on a pull request, claim and risk-acceptor are the two that carry least in a small team.
candidates.counterexample: A two-person startup adopts the profile for its payments changes. Every record reads: claim 'ready'; risks accepted by 'Ana'; examined by 'Ben'. The fields are filled and identical on forty records; the two that vary (evidence limits, undo path) are what a reader wanted.
candidates.gaming: Template text left in place with one word changed per field.
candidates.recommended_change: Cut 7.3 to evidence and its limits, assumptions, remaining risk, undo or contain, stop criterion, and the conditional no-failure scope; examiner at critical.

candidates.strongest_objection: The proposal already rejects the readiness record as an object, correctly: a readiness board per deployment is the textbook transfer failure, and the native form is progressive delivery with pre-stated evaluation. The objection is that it then keeps 'NORMATIVE, PROFILE' as the label for something it did not adopt.
candidates.counterexample: A team with a mature rollout controller (staged percentages, automatic abort on metrics). Any readiness prose is a worse copy of the rollout configuration; the right record is a link to that configuration.
candidates.gaming: Not applicable if no object is created.
candidates.recommended_change: Label M-13 as not adopted. Add one guide sentence: the rollout configuration and its abort thresholds are the readiness record for a staged deployment; link them.

candidates.strongest_objection: The waiver object assumes a lapsed waiver stops the activity. In software it does not, and 7.4 (c) plus example 5 make a lapsed, still-continuing departure disappear from the list of exceptions in force. The eleven-field object was correctly cut to six, and waiver versus deviation correctly dropped (it depends on configuration-control timing, NPR 7120.5F 3.5.2 a).
candidates.counterexample: Credential-rotation exception expires on 1 March. Nobody renews it; the service still does not rotate. Under 7.4 (c) the index stops listing it. An auditor reading the index on 2 March concludes all services rotate credentials.
candidates.gaming: Review condition instead of a date ('review when the service is replaced'), which never trips 7.4 (c); the proposal concedes this.
candidates.recommended_change: Reword 7.4 (c) so that a lapsed exception stays listed and is marked lapsed; require a date, allowing a review condition only in addition.

candidates.strongest_objection: Five named functions come from organizations with formal authority chains. The proposal's 'functions, not posts' paragraph is the right reduction. Residual risk: listing five role names in the guide invites teams to add five fields.
candidates.counterexample: A solo maintainer fills author, reviewer, challenger, approver, and risk owner with the same name on every record.
candidates.gaming: Role names assigned to rotate through the same three people without anyone doing the function.
candidates.recommended_change: Keep the paragraph but name only the three functions the profile's fields use: who decided, who accepted the risk if different, who examined.

candidates.strongest_objection: The loop in the candidate (telemetry, anomaly, analysis, updated requirement) is the aerospace anomaly-resolution chain. Software's native loop is shorter and already instrumented: alert, incident, postmortem, action items, and the error budget that decides whether feature work stops. The proposal never mentions error budgets, which are the native mechanism by which incidents change behaviour and not only documents.
candidates.counterexample: A small team has one incident a quarter and fixes it in the same pull request as the write-up. A separate incident record with a disposition table duplicates the pull request.
candidates.gaming: Lessons written as generic virtues ('improve monitoring') with a link to an epic.
candidates.recommended_change: Keep 7.5 (a) reworded and 7.5 (b); delete 7.5 (c); let a pull request or issue be the incident record.

candidates.strongest_objection: No transfer objection; adding eleven typed relations would have been the aerospace traceability matrix. The mapping does strain two relations (answers for mitigation, implemented-by for a lesson).
candidates.counterexample: none found: adding no relation cannot make a corpus worse; the strained mappings are advisory.
candidates.gaming: Not applicable.
candidates.recommended_change: Drop the two strained mappings from the registry paragraph instead of blessing them; keep the 'Exception to:' label.

candidates.strongest_objection: One profile instead of five addenda is right. But the profile is the size of the Procedure profile dropped from 0.6.0, has no adopter case, and its public cases come from organizations of tens of thousands with launch irreversibility and loss of life. By the admission test's own terms (observed case, or a reader harmed) most of it is anticipated only. The proposal's own honest fallback, the 4.6 sentence plus guidance with section 7 as a recorded deferred proposal, is the result the evidence supports.
candidates.counterexample: A ten-person adopter reads section 7, sees eight MUSTs sourced from shuttle accidents, and declines KADS as a whole as 'aerospace process', losing the Core.
candidates.gaming: Adopt the profile, define nothing as significant.
candidates.recommended_change: Release the 4.6 sentence, the templates, and guide text now; publish section 7 marked as anticipated-only under the M-20 sentence, or defer it until one adopter has used the templates.

candidates.strongest_objection: Blocks instead of documents is the right native form. The incident outline should be a section of the investigation outline, as the proposal half concedes. The assurance block should say that it may live in a pull request description.
candidates.counterexample: A team copies the assurance block into every pull request template; ninety percent of pull requests carry an unfilled block that reviewers learn to ignore, including on the one that mattered.
candidates.gaming: Block present, placeholders unchanged.
candidates.recommended_change: Two additions, not three: the assurance block and the exception outline. Fold incident prompts into templates/investigation.md.

candidates.strongest_objection: RFC 2026 does not support the use made of it: Experimental (4.2.1, read today) is a non-standards-track archive category for research, not a probation for rules, and Proposed Standard 'usually' needs no operational experience. RFC 6410 then cut the ladder to two levels because the three-stage one was not being climbed, which is evidence against maturity ladders, as the proposal's conclusion (no new statuses) already reflects.
candidates.counterexample: none found for the proposed one-sentence form; a six-state lifecycle would have been the counterexample.
candidates.gaming: Every rule is labelled 'anticipated only' forever and never removed.
candidates.recommended_change: Keep the CONTRIBUTING sentence; cite RFC 6410 for the lesson, and remove the claim that RFC 2026 Experimental is the precedent.

candidates.strongest_objection: No transfer objection. The SRE checklist-curation passage is correctly quoted and is a software-native precedent for pruning.
candidates.counterexample: none found: a release-time question with deletion as a valid answer costs minutes.
candidates.gaming: The review is recorded as done with 'no changes'.
candidates.recommended_change: none

candidates.strongest_objection: No transfer objection. It already exists.
candidates.counterexample: none found.
candidates.gaming: Long clauses with many lettered items keep the clause count flat; count lettered requirements, not clauses.
candidates.recommended_change: Count normative sentences or lettered items as well as clauses.

existing_rules_to_challenge.clause_or_artifact: Specification clause 3.5.4 (c) (unexecuted procedure SHOULD say so)
existing_rules_to_challenge.question: would we add this today?
existing_rules_to_challenge.reason: It is the same idea as 3.3.5 (a statement that something was executed says what and when) expressed as a second rule with a different default. The proposal leans on both for recovery paths, which shows they are one rule. Merge into 3.3.5: a procedure presented for use says whether it has been executed as written.

existing_rules_to_challenge.clause_or_artifact: Specification clause 4.6, sentence 'An ADR MAY use its existing identifier with a documented decision-type mapping; it need not also receive a D-prefixed ID.'
existing_rules_to_challenge.question: would we add this today?
existing_rules_to_challenge.reason: It is a mapping permission already given generally by clause 4.3 ('or document a local extension or mapping') and repeated in the decision guide. In a clause that is about to gain another MUST, it is noise. Move to the guide.

existing_rules_to_challenge.clause_or_artifact: Specification clause 5.7 (negative results scoped), research-report profile
existing_rules_to_challenge.question: would we add this today?
existing_rules_to_challenge.reason: 7.3 (i) is the same rule for a different record type. Two profile clauses stating 'a claim of absence says what was inspected' will drift. If 7.3 (i) is admitted, state the principle once in the core next to 3.3.1 (it passes the three-page-repository test: 'not found' needs its scope anywhere) and let 5.7 and 7.3 (i) cite it.

existing_rules_to_challenge.clause_or_artifact: docs/conformance.md, Review outcome: 'An exception MUST record the affected clause identifier and scope, reason, consequence, responsible role, and condition for review.'
existing_rules_to_challenge.question: would we add this today?
existing_rules_to_challenge.reason: Keep, but note the proposal's claim that 7.4 (a) has 'the same six' fields is inexact: conformance asks for consequence, responsible role, and review condition; 7.4 asks for risk accepted, who accepted it, and expiry date or review condition. 'Responsible role' is not 'who accepted the risk'. Either align 7.4 to the conformance wording or admit that it adds fields.

existing_rules_to_challenge.clause_or_artifact: templates/ directory (eleven outlines, including separate conclusion, evidence, question, test, artifact, artifact-bundle)
existing_rules_to_challenge.question: would we add this today?
existing_rules_to_challenge.reason: Software teams hold most of these as native artifacts (test runs, tickets, pull requests). Eleven outlines, about to be thirteen, signal a document-per-thing model that the specification itself disclaims in 3.6.1. Fold conclusion, evidence, question, and test into one 'record' outline with optional sections.

existing_rules_to_challenge.question: would we add this today?
existing_rules_to_challenge.reason: The proposal's own mapping wavers between supported-by and evidenced-by for the same link ('supported-by, or evidenced-by for raw output'). If authors of the standard cannot choose, adopters will not. One relation with the target's nature stated in the link text would answer the same reader question.

dissent_to_preserve: Clause 7.4 (c) as drafted, with worked example 5, removes a still-continuing departure from the list of exceptions in force on the day its acceptance lapses. That reproduces the invisibility the Rogers Commission criticized. If 7.4 (c) is adopted unchanged, this objection should stay on record.

The proposal's finding 2 ('the two shuttle reports describe failures of records') is an interpretation that selects what a documentation standard can fix. The Rogers report says a written recommendation existed and did not reach the deciders; the CAIB's remedy for waivers was an independent authority with sole waiver power (R7.5-1). KADS can decline to build authority, but should not cite these reports as evidence that record rules address the failure.

No rule in section 7 has an observed case in a software team of ordinary size. Every observed case is from an organization with launch irreversibility, loss of life, and a multi-level authority chain, or from Google. Under the admission test these are 'anticipated only' for KADS adopters and the MUSTs are not earned.
Classification by the author at the time of writing is the weakest point of M-11 and no wording fixes it; only classification by kind of change, stated in advance, matches any cited precedent.

Several attributions lend prestige without support and should be corrected before any of this text is published: Vaughan for expiry dates; ISO/IEC/IEEE 15026-2 for a per-change field list; RFC 2026 Experimental for rule probation; RFC 2026 section 6.5 for anything; SRE chapter 15 'unreviewed postmortem' for lesson disposition; principlesofchaos.org for 'not from the absence of incidents'; GitLab for 'actions with owners'; NPR 7123.1D Appendix G for mandatory success criteria (they are 'recommended best practices').

My own verification has limits that should travel with these fact checks: pages were downloaded and searched by string, not read end to end; PDF text extraction scrambles columns so CAIB page numbers are unconfirmed; chapter author names, licences, and the GitLab publication date are from prior knowledge; no paid standard, the Vaughan book, ITIL, NASA-STD-8739.8, or NPR 7150.2D Appendix C was opened.

fact_checks.source: Rogers Commission report, Volume 1, Chapter V
fact_checks.claim_in_proposal: Finding 2 quotation on waiving launch constraints; finding 4 (recommendation reversed 'contrary to the views of its engineers'); deciders 'were unaware ... of the continuing opposition of the engineers'.
fact_checks.correction: All three are exact. Finding 2: 'The waiving of launch constraints appears to have been at the expense of flight safety. There was no system which made it imperative that launch constraints and waivers of launch constraints be considered by all levels of management.' Finding 4: 'the Thiokol Management reversed its position and recommended the launch of 51-L, at the urging of Marshall and contrary to the views of its engineers in order to accommodate a major customer.' Chapter opening, p. 82: 'Those who made that decision were unaware of the recent history of problems concerning the O-rings and the joint and were unaware of the initial written recommendation of the contractor advising against the launch ... and the continuing opposition of the engineers at Thiokol after the management reversed its position.' The proposal's P-09 can now cite the primary page instead of 'a search result'. Overstatements: (a) P-03 says of finding 4 'the GO existed, the supporting claim did not'; the Commission does not say that, and a written Thiokol launch rationale did exist; the finding is about pressure and reversal. (b) The research table says finding 2 supports exceptions being 'time-limited'; finding 2 is about visibility to all management levels only. (c) Finding 2 of 'Three findings' says the reports 'describe failures of records'; note the same sentence on p. 82 says the 'initial written recommendation' existed. The failure the Commission names is that written material did not reach the deciders (finding 3: a 'propensity of management at Marshall to contain potentially serious problems'), which is a propagation and authority failure more than a missing-record failure.

fact_checks.source: Rogers Commission report, Volume 1, Chapter VI
fact_checks.claim_in_proposal: A launch constraint waived for every later flight without the waiver being visible upward; an anomaly accepted because earlier flights had succeeded; a problem closed in tracking on request while unresolved; the eve-of-launch comparison covered only flights with damage; 'normalization of deviance' is not the Commission's wording.
fact_checks.correction: Verified: a launch constraint was placed after STS 51-B; 'Mulloy and Wear both testified that the constraint was still in effect and waived for Challenger's flight'; 'NASA Levels I and II apparently did not realize Marshall had assigned a launch constraint within the Problem Assessment System'; the 51-E Level I review resolution 'acceptable risk because of limited exposure and redundancy'; Figure 6 plots only 'flights with incidents of O-ring thermal distress' and Figure 7 all flights, with the text 'When the entire history of flight experience is considered ... the comparison is substantially different'. The string 'normaliz' does not occur in Chapter VI, so the proposal's caveat is right. Corrections: (1) 'closed in tracking on request while unresolved' compresses a contested account: Thiokol asked for closure on 1985-12-10 ('at Marshall's request according to Brian Russell'), Wear and Mulloy told the Commission they rejected it, and 'two erroneous entries' nevertheless showed the problem 'resolved or closed'. Say 'shown as closed in the tracking report through entries NASA managers called erroneous, after the contractor requested closure'. (2) 'waived for every later flight': my searches confirmed the waiver for 51-L and that upper levels did not know of the constraint; I did not locate the 'each flight' wording, so that part is UNVERIFIED by me.

fact_checks.source: Columbia Accident Investigation Board report, Volume 1
fact_checks.claim_in_proposal: Foam loss reclassified from a requirement violation to an 'in-family', accepted risk as flights returned safely (marked unverified by the proposal); URL https://www.nasa.gov/columbia/caib/.
fact_checks.correction: The claim is supported in substance and can be upgraded from unverified, with two corrections. (1) The URL in the proposal returns HTTP 404 today; use the URLs in this citation. (2) 'In-family' and 'accepted risk' are two separately defined terms used by different offices, not one reclassification: Chapter 6 says bipod foam loss 'came to be treated as in-family, a reportable problem that was within the known experience base, was believed to be understood, and was not regarded as a safety-of-flight issue'; the Integration Office's Hazard Report 37 called it an 'accepted risk' while the External Tank Project called it 'not a safety-of-flight issue', and the Board notes that inconsistency. Also verified: the Board itself attributes the phrase: 'The acceptance of events that are not supposed to happen has been described by sociologist Diane Vaughan as the normalization of deviance' (Chapter 6, note 41), and section 8.2 is titled 'Failures of Foresight: Two Decision Histories and the Normalization of Deviance'. Also relevant and not cited by the proposal: Recommendation R7.5-1, 'Establish an independent Technical Engineering Authority that is responsible for technical requirements and all waivers to them ... Be the sole waiver-granting authority for all technical standards'. The Board's remedy for the waiver problem was an authority, not a record format.

fact_checks.claim_in_proposal: Standard changes are pre-authorized and need no per-change assessment; emergency changes may defer documentation until after the change.

fact_checks.claim_in_proposal: PRR is a service-specific checklist; 'the review did not scale: lead times of quarters and effort proportional to the number of services'. Finding 3: 'direct evidence against any design in which KADS creates a reviewing body or a mandatory review step'. P-01: 'every change must queue for the same review'.
fact_checks.correction: Verified text: 'The checklist is specific to the service'; 'Onboarding each service required two or three SREs and typically lasted two or three quarters. The lead times for a PRR were relatively high (quarters away). The effort level required was proportional to the number of services under review, and was constrained by the insufficient number of SREs available to conduct PRRs.' Overstatements: (1) the PRR in this chapter is a one-time review for SRE taking over operational responsibility for a whole service, not a review per change or per launch; using it in P-01 as a case of 'every change must queue for the same review' misdescribes it. (2) The chapter does not conclude that review should not be required; it says the models were modified (Early Engagement, then 'Frameworks and SRE Platform') so that 'SRE [could] scale their engagement process', and reports 'faster PRR execution' under frameworks. The remedy was to build the reviewed properties into shared infrastructure, which is the native software lesson and one the proposal does not draw. 'Direct evidence against any ... mandatory review step' is firmer than the source.

fact_checks.claim_in_proposal: Advancement requires implementation and operational experience; an Experimental designation exists for work published without that experience.
fact_checks.correction: Verified: 4.1.2 Draft Standard needs 'at least two independent and interoperable implementations ... and ... sufficient successful operational experience'; 4.1.3 Internet Standard needs 'significant implementation and successful operational experience'. But 4.1.1 says 'Usually, neither implementation nor operational experience is required for the designation of a specification as a Proposed Standard', so entry to the standards track needs no experience; only advancement does. 4.2.1 defines Experimental as 'a specification that is part of some research or development effort ... published for the general information of the Internet technical community and as an archival record'; it is a non-standards-track category, not a probationary status for a rule expected to become normative, which is how M-20 uses it. Section 6.5 is 'Conflict Resolution and Appeals' and supports nothing in the stated mechanism; it would be relevant to dissent, and the proposal does not use it there. RFC 6410 confirmed today: 'reduces the Standards Process from three Standards Track maturity levels to two'.
